limits: Plain-language definitions written by eport for orientation. Legal and customs meanings can differ between countries and agreements; where it matters, use the wording of the official source.

terms.definition: A product code from the Harmonized System, the international classification of traded goods run by the World Customs Organization. The first six digits are the same worldwide; countries add more digits for their own tariffs and controls.
A country's own, more detailed product code (often 8 to 10 digits) that sits under an HS heading and carries a specific duty rate and rules.
A tax charged by an importing country on goods entering it, usually worked out from the goods' classification, value and origin.

The value customs uses to calculate duty and taxes on imported goods. It is usually based on the price paid, with adjustments set by the importing country's rules, which follow the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement for its members.
A consumption tax (value-added tax or goods and services tax). Many countries charge it on imports, collected by customs, and many refund or zero-rate it on exports.

Eleven standard trade terms published by the International Chamber of Commerce that set who arranges and pays for transport, insurance and customs clearance, and where risk passes from seller to buyer.
The party that sends the goods and is named as the shipper on the transport document.
The party named on the transport document as the one to receive the goods at destination.
A person or company the carrier should inform when the goods arrive. It does not have to be the consignee.
A company that arranges the movement of goods on behalf of a shipper: booking space with carriers, preparing documents and often handling customs formalities.
A person or firm, often licensed, that prepares and files customs declarations and handles clearance for an importer or exporter.
The carrier's document for sea freight: a receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage and, if negotiable, a document of title.
A non-negotiable transport document for sea freight that names who will receive the goods but is not a document of title.
Twenty-foot equivalent unit: a standard measure of container capacity. A 20-foot container is one TEU and a 40-foot container is two.
Full container load, where one shipper fills a container, and less than container load, where several shippers' goods share one container.

Charges for keeping a container or cargo longer than the free time allowed: demurrage generally applies to time inside the port or terminal, detention to time the container is out of the carrier's control.
Moving goods from one vessel or vehicle to another at an intermediate point on the way to the final destination.
Exporting goods that were earlier imported, usually without substantial change. Re-exports are one reason a seller's and a buyer's trade figures differ.
A treaty between two or more countries or customs territories that reduces or removes duties on trade between them, with rules of origin to decide which goods qualify.
The criteria that decide which country a product comes from for trade purposes, for example where it was wholly obtained or sufficiently processed.
Origin that meets the rules of a specific trade agreement and so qualifies the goods for a reduced or zero duty.
A document stating the country where goods were produced, issued by an authorised body or, under some agreements, replaced by an exporter's declaration.
A system where a limited quantity of a product can be imported at a lower duty rate, and quantities above that are charged a higher rate.
An extra duty a country may charge on imports it finds are sold below normal value and are harming its domestic industry, following an investigation under WTO rules.
A rule other than a customs duty that affects trade in goods, such as licences, quotas, technical regulations, health and safety rules or labelling requirements.
Sanitary and phytosanitary measures protect human, animal and plant health; technical barriers to trade rules cover product standards and conformity assessment. Both are covered by WTO agreements.
A refund or exemption of customs duty on imported materials when the finished goods made with them are exported, where a country offers such a scheme.
A secure facility where imported goods can be stored without paying duty until they are released for the local market or re-exported.
A bank's undertaking, issued at the buyer's request, to pay the seller if documents that comply with its terms are presented.

A payment method where the seller's bank sends documents to the buyer's bank, which releases them to the buyer against payment or acceptance. Unlike a letter of credit, the bank does not promise payment.
A sale where the goods are shipped and documents sent first and the buyer pays later on agreed terms. It carries the most risk for the seller and relies on trust or credit insurance.

A business that a customs administration has recognised as reliable in the supply chain, often entitling it to simpler or faster procedures. Programmes differ by country, and some are recognised between countries.
Items that have both civilian and military or security uses, such as certain electronics, chemicals or software. Exporting them often needs a licence.
Restrictions imposed by governments or international bodies on trade or dealings with certain countries, entities, individuals or goods. They apply on top of ordinary customs rules.
